title: A quick recovery
setting: A weekday morning in the family kitchen. Okaasan and Yuki are getting ready for work when Kenji shuffles in and announces he's too ill for school.

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.romaji: daijoubu? watashi mo kata kotteru. kinou zutto shigoto datta kara.
lines.ja: 大丈夫？私も肩凝ってる。昨日ずっと仕事だったから。
lines.kana: だいじょうぶ？わたしもかたこってる。きのうずっとしごとだったから。
lines.english: You okay? Me too, my shoulders are all stiff. I was working all day yesterday.

lines.speaker: okaasan
lines.romaji: a, kenji, ohayou. mou shichiji han da yo.
lines.ja: あ、ケンジ、おはよう。もう七時半だよ。
lines.kana: あ、けんじ、おはよう。もうしちじはんだよ。
lines.english: Oh, Kenji, morning. It's already half past seven.

lines.speaker: kenji
lines.ja: 今日、学校行かない。お腹痛い。
lines.kana: きょう、がっこういかない。おなかいたい。
lines.english: I'm not going to school today. My stomach hurts.

lines.speaker: okaasan
lines.kana: え、おなかいたいの？だいじょうぶ？
lines.english: Oh no, your stomach hurts? Are you all right?

lines.speaker: kenji
lines.romaji: daijoubu ja nai. atama mo itai shi.
lines.ja: 大丈夫じゃない。頭も痛いし。
lines.kana: だいじょうぶじゃない。あたまもいたいし。
lines.english: No, I'm not. And my head hurts too.

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.romaji: atama mo itai no? nodo wa?
lines.kana: あたまもいたいの？のどは？
lines.english: Your head hurts too? What about your throat?

lines.speaker: kenji
lines.english: My throat... hurts too, I guess?

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.romaji: kana? jibun no nodo da yo?
lines.kana: かな？じぶんののどだよ？
lines.english: You guess? It's your own throat!

lines.speaker: kenji
lines.romaji: itai. a, koshi mo itai. kata mo kotteru.
lines.ja: 痛い。あ、腰も痛い。肩も凝ってる。
lines.kana: いたい。あ、こしもいたい。かたもこってる。
lines.english: It hurts. Oh, and my back hurts. And my shoulders are stiff.

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.romaji: koshi itai no wa okaasan da yo. kata kotteru no wa watashi!
lines.ja: 腰痛いのはお母さんだよ。肩凝ってるのは私！
lines.kana: こしいたいのはおかあさんだよ。かたこってるのはわたし！
lines.english: Mom's the one with the bad back! I'm the one with stiff shoulders!

lines.speaker: okaasan
lines.romaji: demo, okaasan mo yuki mo, shigoto ni iku n da yo.
lines.ja: でも、お母さんもユキも、仕事に行くんだよ。
lines.kana: でも、おかあさんもゆきも、しごとにいくんだよ。
lines.english: And still, Yuki and I are both going to work, you know.

lines.speaker: yuki
lines.romaji: ne, kenji. kyou, karaoke iku n ja nakatta?
lines.ja: ね、ケンジ。今日、カラオケ行くんじゃなかった？
lines.kana: ね、けんじ。きょう、からおけいくんじゃなかった？
lines.english: Hey, Kenji. Weren't you going to karaoke today?

lines.speaker: kenji
lines.english: Oh, karaoke, yeah, I'm going to that.

lines.speaker: okaasan
lines.romaji: onaka mo nodo mo itai n da yo ne? jaa, karaoke mo dame ne.
lines.ja: お腹も喉も痛いんだよね？じゃあ、カラオケもダメね。
lines.kana: おなかものどもいたいんだよね？じゃあ、からおけもだめね。
lines.english: Your stomach and throat hurt, don't they? Then no karaoke either.

lines.speaker: kenji
lines.romaji: onaka mo atama mo, mou itakunai.
lines.ja: お腹も頭も、もう痛くない。
lines.kana: おなかもあたまも、もういたくない。
lines.english: My stomach and my head don't hurt anymore.

lines.speaker: okaasan
lines.ja: じゃあ、学校に行けるね。
lines.kana: じゃあ、がっこうにいけるね。
lines.english: Well then, you can go to school, can't you?

choices.english: Kenji really has a stomachache, so Okaasan lets him stay home from school but says no to karaoke.
Kenji says everything hurts so he can skip school, but once karaoke is off too, he's suddenly fine to go.
Kenji wants to skip karaoke because of his sore throat, so Yuki and Okaasan tell him to rest at home.

questions.explanation: Line 4: Kenji won't go to school because his stomach hurts (kyou, gakkou ikanai. onaka itai). Then the list grows: his head (line 6), his throat, though he isn't sure (line 8: nodo mo, itai kana), and even Okaasan's back and Yuki's shoulders (line 10), which Yuki points out in line 11. Lines 13-14: he still wants to go to karaoke (karaoke wa iku). In line 16 Okaasan says no karaoke either, and in line 17 nothing hurts any more (onaka mo atama mo, mou itakunai), so in line 18 he can go to school. A is wrong: he isn't really ill, since he gets better the moment karaoke is called off, and Okaasan never lets him stay home. C is wrong: Kenji wants to go to karaoke; Okaasan is the one who calls it off.

questions.english: Kenta asks you, "kyou, karaoke iku?" (Coming to karaoke today?) You've got a headache. Say you're not going, and why.
questions.answer: Turn him down and give the reason with atama + itai, adding n da to explain: gomen, kyou wa ikanai. atama itai n da.

modelAnswers.romaji: gomen, kyou wa ikanai. atama itai n da.
modelAnswers.ja: ごめん、今日は行かない。頭痛いんだ。
modelAnswers.english: Sorry, I'm not going today. I've got a headache.

modelAnswers.romaji: sumimasen, kyou wa chotto atama ga itai n desu.
modelAnswers.ja: すみません、今日はちょっと頭が痛いんです。
modelAnswers.english: Sorry, I have a bit of a headache today.

questions.explanation: There is no 'have' in Japanese here: the head is what hurts, atama ga itai, and in casual talk ga drops (atama itai), as in Kenji's line 6 (atama mo itai shi) and Yuki's line 7 (atama mo itai no?). Don't build it with aru or motsu the way English uses 'have'. N da (n desu when polite) turns the headache into your reason for not coming. The second model is the polite version, for someone like Tanaka-san.

questions.english: You put your chopsticks down after a few bites, and Okaasan asks, "e, mou gochisousama? daijoubu?" (What, finished already? Are you okay?) Tell her your stomach hurts.
questions.ja: え、もうごちそうさま？大丈夫？
questions.kana: え、もうごちそうさま？だいじょうぶ？
questions.answer: Say your stomach hurts with onaka + itai, ga dropped in casual talk: un, chotto onaka itai n da.

modelAnswers.romaji: un, chotto onaka itai n da.
modelAnswers.ja: うん、ちょっとお腹痛いんだ。
modelAnswers.english: Yeah, my stomach hurts a bit.

modelAnswers.romaji: uun, daijoubu ja nai. onaka itai.
modelAnswers.ja: ううん、大丈夫じゃない。お腹痛い。
modelAnswers.english: No, I'm not okay. My stomach hurts.

questions.explanation: The everyday tummy ache is onaka ga itai, usually onaka itai in casual talk, as in Kenji's line 4 (onaka itai) and Okaasan's line 5 (onaka itai no?). The dictionary word i (stomach) belongs to medical talk; at the table it's onaka. N da makes it the reason you've stopped eating. The second model answers the daijoubu? part, the way Kenji does in line 6 (daijoubu ja nai).

questions.english: When Kenji says he's still going to karaoke, Yuki says "e? nodo itai noni?" What does she mean?
questions.ja: ユキさんは、何が言いたいですか？
questions.kana: ゆきさんは、なにがいいたいですか？
questions.romaji: yuki-san wa, nani ga iitai desu ka?

choices.english: Singing at karaoke is what made his throat sore in the first place.
She'll go to karaoke in his place so he can rest his voice.
If his throat really hurt, he wouldn't be so keen to go and sing.

questions.explanation: Line 15: nodo itai is a sore throat, and noni is 'even though': 'even though your throat hurts?' A sore throat is exactly what keeps you away from karaoke, so Kenji's quick 'karaoke wa iku' (line 14) gives him away. It fits line 8, where he wasn't even sure his throat hurt (nodo mo, itai kana), and Yuki teased him for it (line 9: kana? jibun no nodo da yo?). A is wrong: nobody says how his throat got sore. B is wrong: Yuki never offers to go, and in line 16 Okaasan calls karaoke off.

questions.english: At the very start, Okaasan groans about where it hurts. What did she say?
questions.ja: お母さんは何と言いましたか？
questions.kana: おかあさんはなんといいましたか？
questions.romaji: okaasan wa nan to iimashita ka?
questions.explanation: Line 1: aa, koshi itai. Koshi is the lower back and hips, the part that aches after lifting or a long day, and what English means by plain 'my back hurts'. B is that English 'back' turned into senaka, which is the upper and middle back, higher than where Okaasan means. C borrows koru from Yuki's stiff shoulders in line 2 (kata kotteru), but Okaasan said itai: her back hurts. Yuki sorts the two out in line 11 (koshi itai no wa okaasan da yo. kata kotteru no wa watashi!).

questions.english: The morning after a long day at your desk, your coworker Mai asks, "kinou, zutto shigoto datta yo ne. daijoubu?" (You were working all day yesterday, right? You okay?) Say you're fine, but your shoulders are stiff.
questions.ja: 昨日、ずっと仕事だったよね。大丈夫？
questions.kana: きのう、ずっとしごとだったよね。だいじょうぶ？
questions.romaji: kinou, zutto shigoto datta yo ne. daijoubu?
questions.answer: Say you're fine, then use kata with the verb koru: un, daijoubu. demo, kata kotteru.

modelAnswers.ja: うん、大丈夫。でも、肩凝ってる。
modelAnswers.english: Yeah, I'm fine. My shoulders are stiff, though.

modelAnswers.romaji: daijoubu desu. demo, chotto kata ga korimashita.
modelAnswers.ja: 大丈夫です。でも、ちょっと肩が凝りました。
modelAnswers.english: I'm fine. My shoulders have got a bit stiff, though.

questions.explanation: English says 'stiff', an adjective, but Japanese uses a verb: kata ga koru. Kotteru means they're stiff now and kotta / korimashita means they've gone stiff; there's no itai in it. That's Yuki's line 2, after a day of work (watashi mo kata kotteru), and Kenji's borrowed complaint in line 10 (kata mo kotteru). The second model is the polite version, for someone like Tanaka-san.

newWords.english: say (nan to iimashita ka? = what did they say?; nani ga iitai? = what are they getting at?)
